source.title: A snake in paradise: Disturbance of plant reproduction following extirpation of bird flower-visitors on Guam

design: Two-island natural experiment: Guam, where the introduced brown treesnake caused severe native bird losses, versus Saipan, where flower-visiting birds remained abundant; two native bird-pollinated plants were measured.

source_native_results.bird_visitation: high on Saipan and zero on Guam
source_native_results.alternative_visitors: insects and lizards visited at low levels; only lizards were considered potential effective alternative pollinators
source_native_results.seed_set: significantly higher on Saipan for both Bruguiera gymnorrhiza and Erythrina variegata var. orientalis
source_native_results.bagging: bagged Bruguiera flowers did not produce viviparous propagules, supporting pollinator dependence

observed_chain: bird extirpation -> zero bird visitation -> reduced seed set in two plant species -> reduced Bruguiera recruitment
why_admitted: the upstream perturbation is a source-defined natural experiment independent of the ABM
the same-direction signal reaches reproduction in two plant species and recruitment in one
the geographic system is independent of the existing strict validation clusters
no state threshold or ABM parameter was selected using these outcomes
claim_boundary: The system validates a qualitative propagation state, not the ABM's specific trait-position generator. Guam and Saipan differ in more than bird abundance, and the brown-treesnake pathway is a particular ecological perturbation rather than a generic island-isolation mechanism.
